fatal_errors: The alloy is incorrectly assumed to be homogeneous, annealed, and single-phase; the studied material was as-cast and contained segregated W-Ta-rich and Zr-Ti-rich regions forming two BCC phases.
The proposed 1000–1200 °C tensile and creep regime is outside the reported room-temperature-to-500 °C quasi-static measurements and cannot support reconstruction of the observed behavior.
A side-by-side comparison of compositionally and microstructurally different materials does not isolate lattice distortion as the causal variable.

The claim that severe lattice distortion lowers barriers to dislocation motion conflicts with the reported interpretation of lattice distortion and W/Ta frictional resistance as strengthening mechanisms.
No supporting prior evidence is cited, and the response extrapolates to sustained service and creep despite the absence of irradiation, creep, or operating-fusion-environment tests.
explanation: The response captures only the broad qualitative expectation that WTaTiVZr may be more ductile and damage tolerant than commercial tungsten. It misses the actual as-cast, dual-BCC dendritic structure, the specific room-temperature compression, room-temperature-to-500 °C indentation, and room-temperature scratch-toughness comparisons, as well as the measured transition in cracking above 200 °C and the quantitative strength and toughness advantages. Its proposed mechanism is generic and partly reversed relative to the paper: lattice distortion was associated mainly with strength, whereas improved plasticity and crack resistance were tentatively associated with Ti, V, and Zr effects, localized deformation, grain-boundary cohesion, and impeded crack propagation. TEM observations could test whether dislocation activity differs, but the proposed experiment cannot attribute such differences specifically to lattice distortion without matched microstructures or controlled compositional/phase variants.
